subject: maths
title: Chapter 8 · Test 1
summary: Chapter 8 test 1: 15 questions on probability, Venn diagrams, two-way tables, conditional and independent events, tree diagrams and counting.
body: This test covers all of Chapter 8: probability review, Venn diagrams and two-way tables, conditional probability, independent events, tree diagrams with and without replacement, and counting techniques. It has 15 multiple-choice questions, from easy to challenge. Allow about 25 minutes, no notes, no calculator unless the question says. Draw a quick tree, table or set of boxes on scrap paper when it helps, and check that every probability you find is between 0 and 1.

questions.prompt: A bag holds 7 red, 5 green and 8 black jellybeans. One is taken at random. What is the probability that it is NOT black?
questions.explanation: There are 20 jellybeans and 12 are not black, so P = 12/20 = 3/5.

mistakes.B: Step 3: 2/5 is the probability that it IS black. Use the complement.
mistakes.C: Step 2: you counted colours (2 of 3 colours). Count the items, not the colours.
mistakes.D: Step 3: you divided by the 8 black jellybeans. A probability is out of the total, 20.

questions.prompt: The Venn diagram shows 25 people and whether they chose Bus and/or Train. One person is picked at random. Find P(Bus ∪ Train).
questions.explanation: Bus ∪ Train is everything inside the circles: 9 + 4 + 6 = 19, so P = 19/25.
steps: ∪ means "or": every region inside either circle.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 4 is the overlap, Bus ∩ Train. ∪ means everything inside either circle.
mistakes.C: Step 2: you left out the overlap. People in both circles are in the union too.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 13 is the whole Bus circle. Add the "Train only" region as well.

questions.diagram_alt: A Venn diagram with ξ = 25: Bus only 9, both 4, Train only 6, and 6 outside both circles

questions.prompt: The probability that a train is on time is 0.9 and, independently, the probability that a bus is on time is 0.7. Find the probability that both are on time.
questions.explanation: The events are independent, so multiply: 0.9 × 0.7 = 0.63. Adding the probabilities is the common slip.
steps: The two events don't affect each other: independent.

mistakes.A: Step 2: you added the probabilities. For "and" with independent events, multiply — a probability can't be more than 1.
mistakes.B: Step 2: that is only the first event. Both must happen, so multiply by the second probability.
mistakes.D: Step 2: that is only the second event. Both must happen, so multiply by the first probability.

questions.prompt: A school uniform is made of a shirt (3 styles), a jumper (2 styles) and pants (4 styles), as shown by the boxes. How many different uniforms are possible?
questions.explanation: Multiplication principle: 3 × 2 × 4 = 24. Adding gives far too few.

mistakes.A: Step 2: you added the choices. Each choice goes with every other choice — multiply.
mistakes.B: Step 2: you forgot the third choice (Pants). Multiply all three boxes.
mistakes.C: Step 2: you added the pants choices at the end. Every box multiplies.

questions.diagram_alt: Three boxes marked ? for the number of choices, labelled Shirt, Jumper and Pants, with multiplication signs between them

questions.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled and the numbers added; the diagram shows every sum. What is the probability that the sum is 6?
questions.explanation: 5 of the 36 equally likely cells fit (1+5, 2+4, 3+3, 4+2, 5+1), so P = 5/36 = 5/36. The 11 sums are not equally likely.

mistakes.B: Step 2: you counted each pair once (e.g. only one of 1 + 5 and 5 + 1). Every cell is a different outcome — count all 5.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the 11 sums are not equally likely. Use the 36 cells.
mistakes.D: Step 1: you put 5 cells over 11 sums. The total is the 36 equally likely cells.

questions.diagram_alt: A 6 by 6 grid with dice values 1 to 6 along the top and side; each cell shows the sum of the two values

questions.prompt: The two-way table has some blank cells. Complete it, then find the probability that a randomly chosen person from all 80 is in the "Year 10" row and the "Home" column (marked ?).
questions.explanation: Year 10 / Canteen = 30 − 18 = 12, so the ? cell = 35 − 12 = 23 and P = 23/80 = 23/80.
steps: Divide by the grand total: P = 23/80.

mistakes.A: Step 3: you divided by the Year 10 row total. The person is chosen from all 80.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 12 is the Year 10 / Canteen cell. Go on to the Home column.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 50 is the whole Home column. You need the Year 10 row only.

questions.diagram_alt: A two-way table with columns Canteen, Home, Total and rows Year 9, Year 10, Total. Year 9: Canteen 18, Total 45. Year 10: Home marked ?, Total 35. Total row: Canteen 30, grand total 80. Other cells blank

questions.prompt: Use the two-way table. A person in the "Senior" row is chosen at random. What is the probability that they are in the "Car" column?
questions.explanation: Given Senior, use only that row: 20 of its 40 are Car, so P = 1/2. Dividing by the grand total ignores the condition.
steps: Given "Senior": use only that row, 40 people.

mistakes.A: Step 1: you divided by all 80. Given "Senior", divide by that row's total.
mistakes.B: Step 1: you divided by the Car column — that is P(Senior | Car). The given group is the Senior row.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 44/80 ignores the condition. Use only the Senior row.

questions.diagram_alt: A two-way table with columns Bus, Car, Total and rows Junior (16, 24, 40), Senior (20, 20, 40) and Total (36, 44, 80)

questions.topic: Tree diagrams with and without replacement
questions.prompt: A raffle has 10 tickets left: 6 belong to Year 9 students and 4 to Year 10 students. Two tickets are drawn without replacement. Find the probability that both belong to Year 10 students.
questions.explanation: Without replacement: 4/10 × 3/9 = 2/15. Using 4/10 twice forgets that the first one is not put back.
steps: Second pick: 9 left, 3 of the right type: 3/9.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 4/10 again is WITH replacement. One has gone, so use 3/9.
mistakes.B: Step 2: you changed the top but not the bottom. Only 9 are left.
mistakes.C: Step 3: you added the branches. Along a path, multiply.

questions.prompt: Six photos are placed in a row, and the class photo must go first. How many different orders are possible?
questions.explanation: Fix the restricted item (1 way), then arrange the other 5: 5! = 120. 6! ignores the rule.
steps: Fill the restricted position first: 1 way.

mistakes.B: Step 1: 6! counts every order. The fixed item has only 1 place.
mistakes.C: Step 2: you subtracted from the total, which counts the orders that break the rule.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 5 items are left, but they can be arranged in many orders — use a factorial.

questions.prompt: Of 50 students, 28 play a sport, 20 play a musical instrument and 10 do neither. One student is chosen at random. What is the probability that they play a sport AND an instrument?
questions.explanation: 50 − 10 = 40 are in at least one group, but 28 + 20 = 48, so 48 − 40 = 8 are counted twice: they are in both. P = 4/25.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 10 is the number in neither group. Use it to find the overlap.
mistakes.C: Step 3: 40/50 is P(at least one). "Both" is only the overlap.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 28 + 20 counts the "both" people twice — compare it with 40.

questions.prompt: P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A ∪ B) = 0.8. Find P(A | B).
steps: Addition rule: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∪ B) = 0.3.

mistakes.A: Step 3: dividing by P(A) gives P(B | A). The given event is B.
mistakes.B: Step 2: that is P(A ∩ B). Divide it by P(B).
mistakes.D: Step 3: you divided by P(A ∪ B). Divide by the given event, P(B).

questions.topic: Tree diagrams with and without replacement
questions.prompt: Zoe sits two tests. P(passes test 1) = 0.7. If she passes test 1, P(passes test 2) = 0.8; if she fails test 1, P(passes test 2) = 0.5 (see the tree diagram). Find the probability that she passes exactly one test.
steps: Exactly one happens on two paths: Pass then Fail, or Fail then Pass.

mistakes.A: Step 3: that is only one path. The other order also gives exactly one — add both paths.
mistakes.B: Step 1: that path has two successes. You need exactly one.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 1 − P(none) is "at least one", which includes two successes.

questions.diagram_alt: A tree diagram: first Pass 0.7 and Fail 0.3; after Pass, Pass 0.8 and Fail 0.2; after Fail, Pass 0.5 and Fail 0.5

questions.prompt: A house has 3 smoke alarms. Each one detects smoke with probability 0.7, independently. Find the probability that at least one alarm detects the smoke.

mistakes.B: Step 2: that is the chance they ALL succeed. "At least one" is 1 − P(none).
mistakes.C: Step 3: that is P(none). Subtract it from 1.
mistakes.D: Step 2: you added the probabilities. Use 1 − P(none) for "at least one".

questions.prompt: Sam drives to work with probability 0.7, otherwise he catches the bus. If he drives, P(late) = 0.1; if he catches the bus, P(late) = 0.3 (see the tree diagram). Sam is late one day. What is the probability that he drove?

mistakes.A: Step 3: 0.1 is P(Late | Drive), the condition the wrong way round. Here Late is given.
mistakes.C: Step 3: 0.07 is P(Drive and Late). Divide it by P(Late).
mistakes.D: Step 3: that is P(Bus | Late), the other branch. Use the Drive path on top.

questions.diagram_alt: A tree diagram: first Drive 0.7 and Bus 0.3; after Drive, Late 0.1 and On time 0.9; after Bus, Late 0.3 and On time 0.7

questions.prompt: Two students are chosen at random from a group of 6 to give a speech. What is the probability that Ava and Leo are the two chosen?
questions.explanation: Number of possible pairs = 6 × 5 ÷ 2 = 15, and only one of them is the pair wanted, so P = 1/15.
steps: Each pair is counted twice (in two orders), so there are 30 ÷ 2 = 15 pairs.
Only one pair is the one wanted: P = 1/15.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 6 × 5 counts ordered picks, but the pair can be picked in 2 orders. Divide by 2 first.
mistakes.B: Step 1: 2/6 is the chance that ONE particular person is chosen. Both must be chosen.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 6 × 6 lets the same person be picked twice. Count pairs of different people.
